extracted.intended_audience: readers of Roman history; students of historiography and classical literature
extracted.subtask_description: Producing or evaluating historical/biographical narrative of Roman events and persons, with attention to character portrayal, legacy, and persuasive/strategic detail. Suitable for creative or scholarly treatments of historical material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historian should record characters as well as persons
rubrics_metrics.description: "As these exhibit their persons, why not the historian their characters?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage argues historians ought to portray the moral and psychological character of individuals, not merely their physical presence or public honors. Emphasize character-sketches that explain motives and dispositions alongside factual acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartial posterity repays just praise
rubrics_metrics.description: "Impartial posterity to every man repays his proper praise"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trust that an impartial future readership will judge actions and attribute praise appropriately; thus authors should aim for truthful, balanced accounts that posterity can use to evaluate reputation. Use accuracy and context so future readers can assess merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censorship/punishment often amplifies a work's credit
rubrics_metrics.description: "The punishment of writers exalts the credit of the writings: nor did ever foreign kings, or any else, reap other fruit from it, than infamy to themselves, and glory to the sufferers."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warnings about suppression: banning or punishing texts frequently increases interest and esteem for them. Writers and historians should be aware that persecution can paradoxically bolster a work's authority and fame — useful when considering the reception and rhetorical framing of controversial material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on enduring virtues rather than monuments
rubrics_metrics.description: "As to temples and statues of stone, if the idol adored in them comes to be hated by posterity, they are despised as his sepulchres."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material honors (temples, statues) are ephemeral if the subject's reputation fails; narrators should foreground actions and virtues (watchfulness, public service, courage) that sustain memory rather than relying on descriptions of honors alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify virtues worthy of remembrance
rubrics_metrics.description: "They will do abundant right to my memory, if they believe me to have been worthy of my ancestors; watchful of the Roman state; unmoved in perils, and in maintaining the public interest, fearless of private enmities."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When crafting legacy or epitaph-like passages, highlight concrete civic virtues (loyalty to ancestors, vigilance for the state, steadiness in danger, prioritizing public interest, fearlessness of private grudges) as criteria by which posterity will judge a life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid portraying universal adoration as true glory
rubrics_metrics.description: "The glory too of Augustus will vanish, if by the promiscuous courtship of flattery it comes to be vulgarly prostituted."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authentic reputation is degraded by indiscriminate flattery; present praise and honors with attention to their sincerity and context. Distinguish genuine acclaim from self-interested or excessive flattery in narrative evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles for persuasive civic petitions and honors
rubrics_metrics.description: Cities or petitioners should appeal to antiquity, past service to Rome, legal/precedential decisions, and demonstrable benefits (e.g., safety from earthquakes, fertility of land, past naval or military aid).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text shows the rhetorical/argumentative elements effective in petitions for honors: cite ancient origins, historical acts of service, legal precedents and prior adjudications, physical suitability (stable ground), and tangible past generosity. Use documented examples and precedents to strengthen claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military/siege narrative principles (tactics and human effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions emphasize tightening entrenchments, depriving water/forage, using bulwarks and missiles, night attacks to create confusion, and the psychological effects of thirst, discord, and despair among the besieged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For vivid and credible military scenes, include methodical operational details (siege lines, reducing supply, engineering works), sensory detail (stench, putrefaction, thirst), and the moral/psychological fragmentation among defenders (surrender vs. suicide). Also depict command measures (strengthening guards, avoiding deception) to show leadership decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character detail as political evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Accounts of court behavior, rumors, and private gestures (e.g., Sejanus covering Tiberius in the cave; Tiberius offering apples to test Agrippina) function as evidence for political motive and public perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specific anecdotes, gestures, and rumors to illuminate political dynamics and character motivations. Small scenes and symbolic acts can serve as convincing evidence for broader claims about ambition, suspicion, and influence; show rather than merely assert motives.
